gloss: A very high, steep piece of land, much taller than a hill.
examples: We hiked to the top of the *mountain* before noon.
The *mountains* were still covered in snow in May.
There's a cabin about halfway up the *mountain*.

gloss: A raised area of land, lower and less steep than a mountain.
examples: Their house sits on a *hill* overlooking the river.
The road climbs a series of steep *hills*.
We sledded down the *hill* behind the school.

gloss: The low land between hills or mountains, often with a river running through it.
examples: The whole *valley* fills with fog in the early morning.
Most of the farms in this *valley* grow corn.
Two *valleys* meet just south of town.

gloss: A deep, narrow valley with steep rock walls, usually cut by a river.
examples: The trail drops a thousand feet into the *canyon*.
You can hear your own echo across the *canyon*.
Narrow *canyons* like this one flood fast when it rains upstream.

gloss: A narrow valley with steep sides, usually with a stream at the bottom.
examples: A wooden bridge crosses the *gorge* at its narrowest point.
The river cut this *gorge* over millions of years.
Both *gorges* are closed to hikers in winter.

gloss: A small, steep-sided valley cut into the ground by running water.
examples: The dog chased a rabbit down into the *ravine*.
Rainwater drains into a *ravine* behind the houses.
We followed the *ravine* until it opened onto a meadow.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, which rhymes with *seen*, not *wine*: ruh-VEEN.

gloss: The pointed top of a mountain.
examples: Three snowy *peaks* rise above the tree line.
Clouds hid the *peak* all afternoon.
From here you can see the highest *peak* in the state.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *peek* (быстро взглянуть).

gloss: The highest point of a mountain.
examples: They reached the *summit* just after sunrise.
The last mile to the *summit* is all loose rock.
Bad weather turned us back well below the *summit*.

gloss: A long, narrow strip of high land along the top of hills or mountains.
examples: The trail follows the *ridge* for about four miles.
The wind hits hard once you're up on the *ridge*.
A line of pines grows along the *ridge*.

gloss: A surface of ground that goes up or down at an angle.
examples: Wildflowers cover the southern *slope* in June.
The *slope* was too steep to drive up.
They planted grapes on the *slopes* above the lake.

gloss: A steep cliff or bank, especially one above a river or the sea.
examples: The old lighthouse stands on a *bluff* above the bay.
Erosion has eaten away part of the *bluff*.
We watched the sunset from the *bluffs*.

gloss: A hill of sand formed by the wind, usually near a beach or in a desert.
examples: The kids were rolling down the *dunes* all afternoon.
A boardwalk crosses the *dune* to the beach.
The wind slowly moves these *dunes* inland.
contrast: Americans say DOON; the British say DYOON.

gloss: A large round hole in the ground made by an explosion, an impact, or a volcano.
examples: A shallow lake fills the old *crater*.
The meteor left a *crater* half a mile wide.
Steam rises from the *crater* on clear mornings.

gloss: A large natural hole in the side of a hill or under the ground.
examples: Bats live in the *cave* year-round.
We took a flashlight into the *cave*.
Early people painted animals on the walls of these *caves*.

gloss: A very large rock, especially one that has been moved by water or ice.
examples: A *boulder* the size of a car blocked the road.
The kids were climbing on the *boulders* by the creek.
We ate lunch in the shade of a *boulder*.
contrast: Pronounced exactly like *bolder* (смелее).

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The hard solid material the earth is made of, or a piece of it.
examples: She skipped a flat *rock* across the pond.
The trail is nothing but loose *rocks* for a mile.
They blasted through solid *rock* to build the tunnel.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A small piece of rock, or rock used as a building material.
examples: He picked up a smooth *stone* and put it in his pocket.
The wall is built of *stones* with no mortar at all.
The old church is made of gray *stone*.

gloss: A small, smooth stone found on a beach or in a stream.
examples: The beach is covered in gray *pebbles*.
A *pebble* got stuck in my shoe.
She tossed a *pebble* into the water and watched the rings spread.

gloss: Small stones used to make paths, roads, and driveways.
examples: Their driveway is *gravel*, not pavement.
The truck kicked up *gravel* as it pulled away.
We spread fresh *gravel* around the shed.

gloss: The sloping side of a hill.
examples: Sheep were grazing on the *hillside*.
The fire burned a whole *hillside* of brush.
Their vineyard runs down the *hillside* to the road.

gloss: A line or group of mountains or hills.
examples: The *range* runs north to south for three hundred miles.
Snow stays on the higher *ranges* into July.
A storm was building over the coastal *range*.

gloss: A mass of earth and rock that slides suddenly down a slope.
examples: A *landslide* closed the highway for three days.
Heavy rain triggered *landslides* all over the county.
You can still see where the *landslide* tore through the trees.

gloss: The solid surface of the earth that you walk on.
examples: The *ground* was still frozen in early April.
He dropped his keys on the *ground*.
Roots spread out just under the *ground*.

gloss: The top layer of earth that plants grow in.
examples: This *soil* is too sandy for tomatoes.
They tested the *soil* before planting anything.
Rich, dark *soil* covers the whole valley floor.

gloss: Loose earth or soil, especially the kind that makes things dirty.
examples: The kids came in with *dirt* all over their knees.
He turned over the *dirt* with a shovel.
Rain turned the *dirt* to mud within an hour.

gloss: Wet, soft earth.
examples: My boots were caked in *mud*.
The truck got stuck in the *mud* by the gate.
After the storm the whole yard was *mud*.

gloss: Heavy, sticky earth that becomes hard when it is dried or baked.
examples: The *clay* here holds water and drains slowly.
She shaped a bowl out of red *clay*.
Nothing grows well in this heavy *clay*.

gloss: Soil or ground, the material that plants grow in.
examples: He dug a hole and packed the *earth* back down.
The smell of damp *earth* filled the air after the rain.
They covered the seeds with a thin layer of *earth*.

gloss: The solid part of the earth's surface, as opposed to the sea.
examples: After six weeks at sea they finally sighted *land*.
His family has farmed this *land* for a century.
Most of the *land* east of the river is protected.

gloss: Land of a particular kind, thought of in terms of its physical features.
examples: The *terrain* gets rocky past the second bridge.
This truck handles rough *terrain* well.
Flat, open *terrain* makes the wind feel colder.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: tuh-RAYN, not TER-rayn.

gloss: Everything you can see when you look across an area of land.
examples: The *landscape* changes completely once you cross the pass.
She paints desert *landscapes*.
Wind turbines have changed the *landscape* around here.

gloss: The natural features of an area, especially when they are beautiful.
examples: The drive is slow, but the *scenery* is worth it.
We kept stopping to take pictures of the *scenery*.
You get better *scenery* on the north side of the lake.

gloss: The line where the land or sea seems to meet the sky.
examples: A ship appeared on the *horizon* just before dark.
The sun was already below the *horizon*.
You can see storms coming from miles off on a flat *horizon*.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable: huh-RY-zuhn, not HOR-ih-zuhn.

gloss: The height of a place or object above sea level.
examples: At this *altitude* the air is noticeably thinner.
The trail gains two thousand feet of *altitude* in three miles.
Some people get headaches at high *altitude*.
contrast: Americans say AL-tih-tood; the British say AL-tih-tyood.

gloss: A large area of flat land with few trees.
examples: The road runs straight across the *plain* for fifty miles.
Herds of bison once covered these *plains*.
A thunderstorm was visible far out on the *plain*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *plane* (самолёт).

gloss: A wide area of flat grassland in North America.
examples: Tall grass covered the *prairie* as far as you could see.
Their farm sits on open *prairie*.
The *prairies* turn gold in late summer.

gloss: A large dry area with little rain and almost no plants.
examples: Nights in the *desert* get surprisingly cold.
They drove across the *desert* at night to avoid the heat.
Some of the world's *deserts* are growing every year.
contrast: The noun is DEZ-urt; the verb *desert* (покинуть) is dih-ZURT, and so is *dessert* (десерт).

gloss: The flat, treeless land in the far north where the ground stays frozen.
examples: Nothing but moss and low shrubs grows on the *tundra*.
Caribou cross the *tundra* twice a year.
The *tundra* thaws only a few inches deep in summer.

gloss: A wide, flat grassland in a hot region, with a few scattered trees.
examples: Elephants move across the *savanna* looking for water.
The *savanna* turns brown in the dry season.
Acacia trees dot the open *savanna*.

gloss: An open piece of land, usually used for growing crops or keeping animals.
examples: The *field* behind the barn is planted in soybeans.
Cows were standing in the far *field*.
We cut through a *field* to get back to the road.

gloss: A field covered in grass and wildflowers.
examples: A creek runs along the edge of the *meadow*.
Deer come out into the *meadow* at dusk.
The high *meadows* are full of flowers in July.
contrast: The *ea* is /e/ as in *bed*: MED-oh, never MEE-doh.

gloss: A field of grass where farm animals feed.
examples: The horses are out in the back *pasture*.
He moves the cattle to a new *pasture* every week.
Half the farm is *pasture* and half is corn.

gloss: The common green plant with thin leaves that covers lawns and fields.
examples: The *grass* is knee-high along the fence.
We sat on the *grass* and waited for the fireworks.
Rain finally turned the *grass* green again.
contrast: Americans say GRAS, rhyming with *pass*; the British say GRAHSS.

gloss: A large wild area of land where no one lives and nothing is farmed.
examples: They spent a week in the *wilderness* with no phone service.
This part of the state is still true *wilderness*.
The trail leaves the road and heads straight into the *wilderness*.
contrast: The first syllable is WIL- with a short /ɪ/, not WYLD- as in *wild*.

gloss: Land outside cities and towns, with farms, fields, and small villages.
examples: We drove through miles of open *countryside*.
She grew up in the *countryside* south of here.
The *countryside* is beautiful in the fall.
contrast: The *cou* is /ʌ/ as in *cut*: KUN-tree-syd, not KOWN-tree-syd.

gloss: A large area thickly covered with trees.
examples: A dirt road cuts through the *forest*.
Most of the state's *forests* are protected.
It gets dark early inside the *forest*.

gloss: A thick tropical forest with dense plants growing close together.
examples: The village is a two-day walk into the *jungle*.
Everything in the *jungle* was wet and green.
They cleared a strip of *jungle* for a landing strip.

gloss: A dense forest in a warm region that gets very heavy rainfall.
examples: The *rainforest* here gets over a hundred inches of rain a year.
Logging has cut into the *rainforest* for decades.
Half the world's species live in tropical *rainforests*.

gloss: A small group of trees growing together, often planted for fruit.
examples: There's an orange *grove* just past the county line.
We parked in the shade of an olive *grove*.
Cold weather ruined half the *groves* that winter.

gloss: A woody plant smaller than a tree, with branches close to the ground.
examples: A rabbit darted under the *bush*.
The *bushes* along the fence need trimming.
Berries grow on low *bushes* all through these woods.
contrast: The vowel is /ʊ/ as in *put*, not /ʌ/ as in *but*.

gloss: A soft green plant that grows in a flat layer on damp rocks and trees.
examples: *Moss* covers the north side of every trunk.
The stones by the creek are slick with *moss*.
Thick *moss* grows on the roof of the old cabin.

gloss: An open space in a forest where there are no trees.
examples: We pitched the tent in a small *clearing*.
A deer stepped out into the *clearing*.
There are two *clearings* along the trail where you can camp.

gloss: A rough path through the countryside or the woods.
examples: The *trail* to the falls is about two miles.
Bikes aren't allowed on this *trail*.
Several *trails* start from the same parking lot.

gloss: A narrow way for walking, made by people or animals.
examples: A stone *path* leads from the porch to the garden.
We followed a deer *path* through the brush.
The *paths* get muddy after a heavy rain.
contrast: Americans say PATH, rhyming with *math*; the British say PAHTH. The plural *paths* ends in a voiced /ðz/.

gloss: A large area of salt water, smaller than an ocean.
examples: The *sea* was rough all week.
Their house looks out over the *sea*.
He spent thirty years at *sea*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *see* (видеть).

gloss: One of the very large areas of salt water that cover most of the earth.
examples: We could hear the *ocean* from the porch.
Plastic ends up in the *ocean* no matter where you throw it away.
The world's *oceans* are warming faster than expected.

gloss: A large area of water surrounded by land.
examples: The *lake* freezes solid by January.
We rented a cabin on the *lake*.
There are hundreds of small *lakes* in this part of the state.

gloss: A small area of still water, smaller than a lake.
examples: Frogs sing by the *pond* every night in spring.
He keeps ducks on a little *pond* behind the house.
Both *ponds* dried up during the drought.

gloss: A large natural stream of water flowing toward the sea or a lake.
examples: The *river* runs right through downtown.
Two *rivers* meet just north of the bridge.
Heavy rain pushed the *river* over its banks.

gloss: A small, narrow river.
examples: A cold *stream* runs behind the cabin.
We crossed three *streams* on the way up.
The *stream* dries up completely by August.

gloss: A small stream.
examples: The kids caught crawfish in the *creek*.
Our property line follows the *creek*.
Several *creeks* feed into the river here.
contrast: *Creek* is the everyday American word for a small stream; British English usually says *stream* or *brook*.

gloss: A small stream, especially one in the woods or a meadow.
examples: A *brook* runs along the bottom of the field.
You can hear the *brook* from the back bedroom.
Two *brooks* join just below the old mill.

gloss: A place where water flows naturally out of the ground.
examples: The town's water comes from a mountain *spring*.
Hot *springs* bubble up all along the fault.
We filled our bottles at a *spring* beside the trail.

gloss: A place where a river or stream falls over a steep drop.
examples: You can hear the *waterfall* long before you see it.
The *waterfall* freezes into a column of ice each winter.
There are three *waterfalls* along this stretch of river.

gloss: A stretch of river where the water runs fast over rocks.
examples: We carried the canoe around the *rapids*.
The *rapids* below the bridge are dangerous in spring.
He's run these *rapids* dozens of times.
contrast: Always plural: *the rapids*, never "a rapid".

gloss: A long, narrow channel dug to carry water or boats.
examples: Barges still move grain along the *canal*.
The *canal* was drained for repairs.
A network of *canals* irrigates the whole valley.

gloss: A lake, often man-made, where water is stored for later use.
examples: The *reservoir* is down twenty feet after two dry years.
Fishing is allowed on the lower *reservoir*.
The city gets its drinking water from three *reservoirs*.
contrast: The French ending *-voir* is said VWAHR: REZ-ur-vwahr.

gloss: The whole area of land that drains into a particular river, or a wide hollow in the land.
examples: Snowmelt from the whole *basin* feeds this river.
The town sits in a shallow *basin* between two ridges.
Rainfall across the *basin* has dropped five years running.

gloss: A stream or river that flows into a larger one.
examples: This creek is a *tributary* of the river that runs through town.
Dozens of small *tributaries* feed the lake.
Pollution in one *tributary* affects the whole system.

gloss: A small pool of water lying on the ground after rain.
examples: The kids jumped in every *puddle* on the way home.
A *puddle* had formed at the bottom of the driveway.
By noon the *puddles* had dried up.

gloss: A natural spring that shoots hot water and steam into the air.
examples: The *geyser* goes off about every ninety minutes.
Steam drifts over the *geysers* all morning.
We waited an hour to watch the *geyser* erupt.
contrast: Americans say GY-zur; the British say GEE-zur.

gloss: A part of the sea or a lake that curves into the land.
examples: Sailboats filled the *bay* all weekend.
Fog rolls in across the *bay* most evenings.
Small *bays* along this coast make good anchorages.

gloss: A small sheltered bay.
examples: We anchored in a quiet *cove* for the night.
There's a swimming beach in the next *cove* over.
Seals haul out on the rocks in these *coves*.

gloss: A narrow strip of water reaching from the sea into the land.
examples: An *inlet* cuts a mile inland from the harbor.
Fishing boats tie up in the *inlet*.
The tide runs fast through the narrow *inlet*.

gloss: A sheltered area of water where ships can stay safely.
examples: Dozens of boats were moored in the *harbor*.
The storm passed and the *harbor* went quiet again.
Both *harbors* are too shallow for large ships.
contrast: American spelling *harbor*; British spelling *harbour*.

gloss: A shallow area of salt water separated from the sea by sand or rock.
examples: The water in the *lagoon* is warm and perfectly still.
A thin strip of sand separates the *lagoon* from the ocean.
Fish spawn in the shallow *lagoons*.

gloss: The land right next to the sea.
examples: We drove up the *coast* as far as the state line.
Storms hit this *coast* every fall.
Both *coasts* were under a wind advisory.

gloss: The land along the edge of a sea, lake, or wide river.
examples: They walked along the *shore* looking for shells.
A row of cabins sits on the north *shore*.
Waves pushed driftwood up onto the *shore*.

gloss: The line where a body of water meets the land.
examples: Erosion has moved the *shoreline* back thirty feet.
The whole *shoreline* is public here.
Both *shorelines* are lined with pines.

gloss: An area of sand or small stones next to the sea or a lake.
examples: The *beach* was empty except for a couple of joggers.
We spent the whole day at the *beach*.
Public *beaches* close at ten.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *beech* (бук, дерево).

gloss: The land along the side of a river or lake.
examples: Willows grow all along the *bank*.
The river rose over its *banks* overnight.
We fished from the far *bank*.
contrast: Identical to *bank* (банк) — only the context tells you which one is meant.

gloss: The flat, fan-shaped area of land where a river splits before entering the sea.
examples: Rice grows all across the *delta*.
The *delta* is crossed by dozens of small channels.
Sediment keeps building up at the mouth of the *delta*.

gloss: The wide part of a river where it meets the sea and fresh water mixes with salt.
examples: Birds stop in the *estuary* on their way south.
Oysters grow well in the *estuary*.
Runoff from the city drains into the *estuary*.

gloss: A narrow passage of water joining two larger areas of sea.
examples: Ferries cross the *strait* every hour.
The *strait* is only three miles wide at that point.
Ice closes the *straits* for part of the winter.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *straight* (прямой).

gloss: A narrow stretch of water between two seas, or the deeper part of a river where boats pass.
examples: The ferry crosses the *channel* in about an hour.
Dredgers keep the shipping *channel* open.
Storms have shifted the *channel* twice in ten years.

gloss: A piece of land that sticks out into the sea.
examples: A lighthouse stands at the end of the *cape*.
We rounded the *cape* just before dark.
The wind hits hard on the far side of the *cape*.

gloss: The regular rise and fall of the sea during the day.
examples: The *tide* comes in fast here, so watch your gear.
We launched the boat at high *tide*.
The *tides* are strongest around a full moon.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *tied* (связанный).

gloss: A raised line of water moving across the surface of the sea.
examples: *Waves* were breaking over the seawall.
One *wave* knocked him right off the board.
The *waves* are usually flat in the morning.

gloss: A steady flow of water moving in one direction in a river or the sea.
examples: The *current* is strong in the middle of the river.
Swimmers get pulled out by the *current* every summer.
Warm ocean *currents* keep this coast mild.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *currant* (смородина).

gloss: The waves breaking on the shore, and the white foam they make.
examples: The *surf* was too rough to swim in.
We could hear the *surf* from the parking lot.
Kids were playing in the *surf* all afternoon.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *serf* (крепостной).

gloss: A plant that grows in the sea, often washed up on the beach.
examples: *Seaweed* covered the whole tide line.
Something was tangled up in the *seaweed*.
They dry the *seaweed* and sell it in thin sheets.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A hard substance formed in warm seas by tiny animals, often brightly colored.
examples: Warmer water is killing the *coral*.
She wore a necklace of red *coral*.
Divers counted a dozen kinds of *coral* on one dive.

gloss: The hard outer covering of a sea creature such as a clam or a snail.
examples: She collected *shells* along the waterline.
A crab was living in an empty *shell*.
The beach is covered in broken *shells*.

gloss: An area of land that is covered with shallow water for much of the year.
examples: The *wetland* filters runoff before it reaches the bay.
Developers drained these *wetlands* fifty years ago.
Herons nest in the *wetland* just east of town.

gloss: Low, soft, wet ground covered with grasses and reeds.
examples: Red-winged blackbirds nest in the *marsh*.
A boardwalk runs out across the salt *marsh*.
The *marshes* flood every spring.

gloss: An area of low, wet ground with trees growing in it.
examples: Cypress trees stand right in the middle of the *swamp*.
Mosquitoes come off the *swamp* by the thousands.
They built a boardwalk through the *swamp*.

gloss: An area of soft, wet, spongy ground made of decaying plants.
examples: Cranberries grow in a *bog* like this one.
My boot came off in the *bog*.
Peat has been building up in these *bogs* for thousands of years.

gloss: A huge mass of ice that moves very slowly down a valley.
examples: The *glacier* has retreated half a mile in twenty years.
Meltwater from the *glacier* feeds the river.
Most of the *glaciers* in the park are shrinking.
contrast: Americans say GLAY-shur; the British say GLASS-ee-ur.

gloss: A very large piece of ice floating in the sea.
examples: An *iceberg* drifted past the harbor entrance.
Most of an *iceberg* sits below the surface.
*Icebergs* break off the glacier every summer.

gloss: Water that has frozen solid.
examples: The *ice* on the pond isn't thick enough to walk on.
Black *ice* made the bridge dangerous.
*Ice* was still floating in the channel in April.

gloss: A large mass of snow and ice that suddenly slides down a mountain.
examples: An *avalanche* buried a mile of the highway.
The *avalanche* risk is high after a heavy snowfall.
Two skiers set off a small *avalanche*.

gloss: A piece of land completely surrounded by water.
examples: The *island* is a forty-minute ferry ride from the mainland.
There are hundreds of small *islands* in the bay.
Only twelve people live on the *island* year-round.
contrast: The *s* is silent: Y-luhnd.

gloss: A piece of land almost surrounded by water, joined to the mainland at one end.
examples: The whole *peninsula* is a state park.
One road runs the length of the *peninsula*.
Both *peninsulas* are popular with birdwatchers.

gloss: One of the seven great masses of land on the earth.
examples: She's been to five *continents* so far.
The two *continents* were joined millions of years ago.
Rail lines cross the *continent* from coast to coast.

gloss: The imaginary line around the middle of the earth, halfway between the poles.
examples: The country sits right on the *equator*.
Days and nights are the same length at the *equator*.
We crossed the *equator* on the third day out.

gloss: Either of the two points at the very top and bottom of the earth.
examples: Ice is melting at both *poles*.
The expedition reached the *pole* in January.
A compass needle points toward the magnetic *pole*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *poll* (опрос).

gloss: A large area of a country or of the world with its own character.
examples: Wine from this *region* is mostly red.
Dry *regions* are getting drier.
The whole *region* was under a flood watch.

gloss: The line separating two countries, states, or areas.
examples: The river forms the *border* between the two states.
We crossed the *border* around midnight.
Both *borders* run through heavy forest.

gloss: The physical world of plants, animals, and landscapes, apart from people.
examples: He'd rather spend a weekend out in *nature* than in a city.
*Nature* takes an abandoned field back within a few years.
Kids need more time outdoors in *nature*.

gloss: The natural world, especially as it is affected by human activity.
examples: The plant was fined for polluting the *environment*.
Plastics stay in the *environment* for centuries.
Voters around here care a lot about the *environment*.
contrast: Stressed on the second syllable, which rhymes with *fire*: in-VY-ruhn-muhnt.

gloss: The natural place where a particular animal or plant lives.
examples: Logging destroyed the owl's *habitat*.
These wetlands are prime *habitat* for migrating birds.
Different *habitats* support very different species.

gloss: All the plants and animals of an area together with the environment they live in.
examples: One invasive species can upset the whole *ecosystem*.
The reef *ecosystem* is recovering slowly.
Coastal *ecosystems* are especially fragile.

gloss: Animals and birds living free in their natural surroundings.
examples: The park is full of *wildlife*.
Slow down at dusk, because that's when *wildlife* crosses the road.
The refuge protects *wildlife* along the whole river.

gloss: Hot liquid rock that flows out of a volcano.
examples: *Lava* was still glowing at the base of the cone.
The village sits on old *lava*.
Cooled *lava* forms sharp black rock.

gloss: A natural solid substance found in the ground, such as quartz or salt.
examples: The rock is full of shiny *minerals*.
This spring water carries a lot of dissolved *minerals*.
They mine a rare *mineral* in the hills north of town.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A piece of a substance that has formed naturally into a regular shape with flat sides.
examples: Ice *crystals* covered the window.
He found a quartz *crystal* the size of his thumb.
Salt dries into fine white *crystals*.

gloss: The remains or shape of an ancient plant or animal preserved in rock.
examples: Kids find *fossils* in the shale along the creek.
The museum has a dinosaur *fossil* in the lobby.
This whole cliff is packed with shell *fossils*.

gloss: A sudden violent shaking of the ground.
examples: The *earthquake* woke everybody up around three in the morning.
Small *earthquakes* happen here almost weekly.
The bridge was rebuilt after the *earthquake*.

gloss: A large amount of water covering land that is usually dry.
examples: The *flood* reached the second floor of some houses.
Spring *floods* are normal along this river.
*Flood* damage ran into the millions.
contrast: The *oo* is /ʌ/ as in *blood*: FLUD, not FLOOD.

gloss: A long period with little or no rain.
examples: The *drought* has lasted three summers now.
Reservoirs are low after a year of *drought*.
Farmers lost most of the crop to the *drought*.
contrast: The *gh* is silent and *ou* is /aʊ/: DROWT, rhyming with *out*.

gloss: A large fire that spreads quickly through forest or grassland.
examples: Smoke from the *wildfire* reached three states.
*Wildfires* start earlier in the year than they used to.
The *wildfire* burned for six weeks before it was contained.

gloss: The space above the earth that you see when you look up.
examples: The *sky* turned orange right before the storm.
There wasn't a cloud in the *sky* all week.
Clear *skies* are forecast through Sunday.

gloss: The time in the morning when the sun appears above the horizon.
examples: We were on the road before *sunrise*.
The *sunrise* over the lake was worth getting up for.
In midsummer *sunrise* comes just after four.

gloss: The time in the evening when the sun goes down below the horizon.
examples: The park closes at *sunset*.
We watched the *sunset* from the end of the pier.
Winter *sunsets* here are early and quick.
